question: Where are managed settings placed on macOS?

options.text: ~/.claude/managed-settings.json
options.explanation: User's home directory — a developer can modify it. Managed settings must not be editable by users

options.text: /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/
options.explanation: System directory requiring root privileges to write. Only an administrator can change managed settings

options.text: /usr/local/etc/claude-code/
options.explanation: This is not the standard path for Claude Code managed settings on macOS

options.text: .claude/managed/
options.explanation: Files in the project directory are available for developer editing — this is not the managed level

options.text: Managed settings become advisory, not mandatory
options.explanation: Managed settings are always mandatory. allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly strengthens control, not weakens it

options.text: Enables managed settings at the project level
options.explanation: Managed settings are set by a system administrator at the OS level, not at the project level

options.text: Allows developers to add their own allow rules on top of managed
options.explanation: The opposite — this parameter prohibits developers from adding their own permission rules

options.text: Only managed policy can define allow rules — developers cannot extend permissions
options.explanation: The organization fully controls what is allowed. A developer cannot add allow for additional tools

question: Why should an organization restrict available MCP servers via managed-mcp.json?

options.text: Cost: each MCP call spends tokens
options.explanation: Uncontrolled use of MCP servers increases API costs — the organization wants to control the budget

options.text: Performance: MCP servers slow down the agent
options.explanation: MCP calls add latency, but this isn't the main reason for restrictions. Security, cost, and compliance are the primary motivators

options.text: Compliance: data must not leak through third-party servers
options.explanation: Regulatory requirements may prohibit transmitting certain data through external services

options.text: Security: not all MCP servers are trusted
options.explanation: A third-party MCP server could be compromised or intentionally malicious — data through it could leak

question: How does path-specific targeting in .claude/rules/ work?

options.text: Paths are specified in the file's frontmatter — rules apply only when working with files matching those paths
options.explanation: Claude loads rules from .claude/rules/ only when working with files matching the paths patterns. For example, backend rules for src/api/**

options.text: Rules execute in the order of files in the directory
options.explanation: Order doesn't depend on file names — rules are activated by path matching, not alphabetically

options.text: Rules are applied to all project files equally
options.explanation: The point of path-specific targeting is different rules for different parts of the project

options.text: Each rules file can contain only one rule
options.explanation: A rules file can contain any number of rules and recommendations for the specified paths

question: A team of 15 is starting to use Claude Code. What's the first step?

options.text: Each developer configures Claude Code independently
options.explanation: Without shared standards, each will generate code in their own style — the codebase will quickly become chaotic

options.text: Install managed policy on all machines
options.explanation: Managed policy is for organizations with security requirements. For a team of 15, start with CLAUDE.md and project settings

options.text: Write 50 skills for all possible tasks
options.explanation: Start with base rules, not skills. Add skills as recurring tasks are identified

options.text: Create CLAUDE.md with base rules and .claude/settings.json with permissions, commit to git
options.explanation: Shared standards are the foundation of team work. CLAUDE.md defines code style, settings.json defines permissions and restrictions

question: Why shouldn't CLAUDE.md be longer than 200 lines?

options.text: It's an Anthropic standard for CLAUDE.md
options.explanation: There's no formal restriction from Anthropic. 200 lines is a practical recommendation for effective context usage

options.text: Git can't store large markdown files
options.explanation: Git handles files of any size just fine. The limitation relates to the agent's context window, not git

options.text: The agent spends context window on reading, and rules/ and skills/ are available for details
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md is read on every launch. The longer it is, the less context remains for work. Details are moved to rules/ (on-path) and skills/ (on-demand)

options.text: Claude Code doesn't support files longer than 200 lines
options.explanation: There's no technical limitation. The problem is context window consumption and reduced accuracy with large volumes

question: What's the advantage of plugins over copying files between projects?

options.text: Standardization: all developers get the same set of tools
options.explanation: A plugin guarantees everyone has the same skills, hooks, and agents — no discrepancies from manual copying

options.text: Plugins run faster than regular files
options.explanation: Performance is the same — a plugin ultimately unpacks to the same files. The advantage is manageability, not speed

options.text: Single source of truth: changes in one place
options.explanation: Fixed a bug in a hook — all projects get the fix on update, no need to search for copies across 20 repositories

options.text: Versioning: you can update a plugin for everyone at once
options.explanation: When a plugin is updated, all projects using it get the new version — no need to update each project manually

options.text: This depends solely on the programming language
options.explanation: This is an architectural decision independent of the language.

question: How does Claude Code use .claude/rules/ when working with files?

options.text: Loads all rules files in every session
options.explanation: That would be wasteful for context. Claude loads only relevant rules based on paths

options.text: Automatically loads only those rules whose paths match the files the agent is working with
options.explanation: If the agent edits src/api/users.ts, rules with paths: ['src/api/**'] are loaded, but not frontend rules

options.text: Rules apply only when skills are invoked
options.explanation: Rules work independently of skills — they're automatically activated when working with files at the specified paths

options.text: The developer must manually specify which rules to apply
options.explanation: Rules are loaded automatically by path matching — no manual specification is required

question: An organization rolled out allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly: true, and developers complain the agent can't run tests. What's the likely cause?

options.text: All Claude Code sessions need to be restarted
options.explanation: Managed settings apply automatically. The problem is in configuration, not caching

options.text: Tests aren't working because of sandbox
options.explanation: Sandbox might block network requests, but running npm test is a permissions issue, not sandbox

options.text: Bash(npm test*) wasn't added to the allow list in the managed policy
options.explanation: allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly prohibits adding allow rules at the project and user levels. If npm test isn't allowed in managed — it's unavailable

options.text: Developers haven't updated Claude Code to the latest version
options.explanation: The problem isn't the version — it's that the managed policy didn't include the necessary allow rules

question: A new developer joins the project. Which combination of Claude Code tools best helps with onboarding?

options.text: Only CLAUDE.md — everything is written there
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md is a good base, but full onboarding needs interactive tools: skills for environment setup, agents for review

options.text: Managed policy with maximum restrictions for newcomers
options.explanation: Strict restrictions will hinder learning. A newcomer needs support (skills, agents), not additional barriers

options.text: A personal CLAUDE.md for each newcomer
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md should be shared for the team. Personal settings go in settings.local.json, but onboarding needs skills and agents

options.text: CLAUDE.md for project understanding + environment setup skill + code review agent
options.explanation: Three levels: CLAUDE.md provides context, skill automates setup, agent helps write code to standards. Together they create an interactive mentor

question: What is allowManagedHooksOnly and why is it needed?

options.text: Automatically creates hooks based on managed policy
options.explanation: The parameter doesn't create hooks — it prohibits adding hooks at levels below managed

options.text: Allows using only built-in Claude Code hooks
options.explanation: The parameter isn't about built-in hooks — it's about who can define hooks: only managed policy or all settings levels

options.text: Hooks only work in managed mode
options.explanation: Hooks work in all modes. allowManagedHooksOnly controls who can define hooks

options.text: Only hooks from managed policy will execute — developers can't add their own
options.explanation: This prevents a situation where a developer creates a hook that bypasses or disables corporate security checks

question: A team wants the agent to always run the linter after finishing work. Which hook to use?

options.text: SessionStart with matcher: '.*'
options.explanation: SessionStart is the beginning of a session, not the end. The linter is needed after changes, not before them

options.text: PreToolUse with matcher: 'Write|Edit'
options.explanation: PreToolUse fires before each edit, not at work completion. Running linter after every Edit is too frequent

options.text: Stop with matcher: '.*'
options.explanation: The Stop hook fires when the agent finishes work. Running the linter at this stage ensures all code is checked

options.text: PostToolUse with matcher: '.*'
options.explanation: PostToolUse after every tool — the linter would run dozens of times per session. Stop — once at completion
